effect_size.excerpt: The pooled (random effects) estimates were: OR=1.11 (95% CI 0.96–1.28) per 10nmol/L folate (P=0.2); OR=1.10 (95% CI 1.01–1.19) per 100pmol/L B 12 (P=0.002); and OR=0.91 (95% CI 0.69–1.19) per 10μmol/L tHcy (P=0.5). cases.excerpt: A study was performed with a nested case-control design based on individual participant data from six cohort studies including 6875 cases and 8104 controls; blood collection from 1981 to 2008, and an average follow-up of 8.9 yr (standard deviation 7.3). Odds ratios (ORs) of incident PCa by study-specific fifths of circulating folate and vitamin B<sub>12</sub> were calculated using multivariable adjusted conditional logistic regression.

effect_size.excerpt: Higher folate and vitamin B<sub>12</sub> concentrations were associated with a small increase in risk of PCa (ORs for the top vs bottom fifths were 1.13 [95% confidence interval (CI), 1.02-1.26], p<sub>trend</sub>=0.018, for folate and 1.12 [95% CI, 1.01-1.25], p<sub>trend</sub>=0.017, for vitamin B<sub>12</sub>), with no evidence of heterogeneity between studies. The association with folate varied by tumour grade (p<sub>heterogeneity</sub><0.001); higher folate concentration was associated with an elevated risk of high-grade disease (OR for the top vs bottom fifth: 2.30 [95% CI, 1.28-4.12]; p<sub>trend</sub>=0.001), with no association for low-grade disease.

confidence_interval.excerpt: Higher folate and vitamin B<sub>12</sub> concentrations were associated with a small increase in risk of PCa (ORs for the top vs bottom fifths were 1.13 [95% confidence interval (CI), 1.02-1.26], p<sub>trend</sub>=0.018, for folate and 1.12 [95% CI, 1.01-1.25], p<sub>trend</sub>=0.017, for vitamin B<sub>12</sub>), with no evidence of heterogeneity between studies.

headline.funnel_interpretation: Egger's test indicates no significant funnel plot asymmetry (p=0.0920). The distribution of studies appears symmetric, suggesting a lower risk of publication bias.
headline.results_interpretation: The pooled analysis of 10 studies yielded an effect size of 1.02 (95% CI: 0.95–1.1), indicating no statistically significant association between folic acid and prostate cancer. Although the point estimate suggests a potential positive relationship, the confidence interval includes the null. These findings were accompanied by moderate heterogeneity (I² = 48.96%), suggesting some variability in the results across studies.
